@UnslothAI just dropped MTP for Qwen 3.7 Flash Next (125B A6B)! 25 tokens/sec on a single RTX 4090!

I took the 125B (6B active) setup from below, plugged in the new shared-Q8_0 MTP drafter, and pushed decode throughput to 25.35 tokens/sec at an 80k context window on a single 24GB RTX 4090.

You must build from @danielhanchen's PR branch (#144):

git clone https://t.co/kGHHf8Zxmg && cd llama.cpp
git fetch origin pull/144/head:mtp && git checkout mtp
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native
cmake --build build -j $(nproc) --target llama-server

# The 80k MTP Benchmark Run

Fed it the same continuous 28k token prompt, combining CPU-MoE offload (-cmoe) with MTP speculative decoding (--spec-draft-n-max 2):

llama.cpp flags: 
./build/bin/llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-model mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-shared-Q8_0.gguf --spec-draft-n-max 2 -c 80000 -cmoe --threads 12 -b 4096 -ub 4096 --port 8080
Prefill: 471.08 t/s (Up from 355.72 t/s baseline, a 32% prefill jump)

Decode: 25.35 t/s (Up from 20.84 t/s baseline)

Footprint: 19.0 GB VRAM | 92 GB DDR4 System RAM

# Why shared-Q8_0 is the Optimal Choice

The shared-Q8_0 MTP head borrows token embeddings and output projections directly from the base model, saving ~1.3GB of critical VRAM. Setting --spec-draft-n-max 2 delivers consistent speculative acceptance without thrashing the PCIe 4.0 bus during offloaded MoE passes.

This is just the initial 80k verification pass. Currently benchmarking the 180,000 and 250,000 deep context runs with MTP active. full scaling data drops soon.

You don't need a GPU for fast studio grade voice cloning anymore. 

Qwen3 TTS (1.7B Q4_K_M) + mainline llama.cpp is officially the fastest way to generate zero shot voice clones using 100% pure CPU execution.

Following up on my last post where we ran the Q8 model on a GPU, we just took local C++ voice synthesis a massive step further. The open source community quantized Alibaba's SOTA Qwen3 TTS model down to Q4_K_M GGUF, completely freeing local audio pipelines from dedicated graphics hardware.

Here is the real world benchmark and hardware breakdown of running SOTA voice cloning on CPU:

# Architecture & Model Setup

Using Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base-Q4_K_M.gguf paired with the 8 bit multimodal projector (mmproj-Q8_0.gguf), llama.cpp executes the entire pipeline in pure C++. No PyTorch, no CUDA dependencies, and no VRAM bottlenecks.

# Real-World Memory Footprint

- Baseline RAM: 1.6 GB system idle. 
- Peak Generation RAM: 8 GB RAM during active voice synthesis. 
- Requirement: Any basic machine with at least 8 GB of system RAM can run this easily.

# Real World CPU Benchmarks

- Google Colab Free Tier (Throttled 2 Core CPU): Synthesizes a 5 sec studio quality audio clip (~8 words) in 45 seconds. 
- Modern Consumer CPU (Intel i5/i7 13th/14th Gen or AMD Ryzen 7000/9000):  generation should drop to 5 to 20 seconds (nearly 1:1 real-time generation speed!).

# Zero Shot Voice Cloning Quality
Pass any 5 to 20 second .wav audio sample to the C++ engine using the --tts-speaker-file flag. It yields clean, natural sounding cloned speech with virtually zero quality loss compared to unquantized FP16 weights.

To make testing seamless, I built an updated zero config Google Colab notebook. It pulls the official pre built llama.cpp CPU binaries (zero compilation time!)

I just ran Qwen 3.8 Flash Next (MoE) 125B A6B with a  250,000 context window on a single 24GB RTX 4090.

21 tokens/sec decode. 364 t/s prefill. 

no mtp. no dflash. no kv cache quantization!

We are running datacenter models on consumer hardware.

Tested on Ubuntu 22 | CUDA 13.0 | PCIe 4.0 x16 | 110 GB DDR4 System RAM with a continuous 28k prompt across all runs.

### The Benchmarks & Scaling

# 1. Hybrid Offload (-ncmoe 40 @ 80k Context)
Offloaded 40 expert layers to the GPU, pushing VRAM to the ceiling.

./build/bin/llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf -c 80000 --port 8080 -v --fit off -b 4096 -ub 4096 -ncmoe 40

Prefill: 383.85 t/s | Decode: 22.52 t/s
Footprint: 23.85 GB VRAM | 97 GB RAM

# 2. Full CPU MoE Offload (-cmoe @ 80k Context)

Pinned all 512 expert layers to DDR4 RAM (-cmoe), keeping attention on the 4090.

llama.cpp flags: (Same as above, replace -ncmoe 40 with -cmoe)

Prefill: 355.72 t/s | Decode: 20.84 t/s
Footprint: 11.66 GB VRAM (12GB+ VRAM freed up!) | 110 GB RAM

# 3. The 180,000 Context Run

Prefill: 357.75 t/s | Decode: 20.98 t/s | VRAM: 15.6 GB | RAM: 110 GB

# 4. The 250,000 Context Absolute Ceiling

./build/bin/llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf -c 250000 --port 8080 -v --fit off -b 4096 -ub 4096 -cmoe

Prefill: 364.29 t/s | Decode: 20.97 t/s

Footprint: 18.3 GB VRAM (Still ~5.7 GB of VRAM headroom!) | 110 GB RAM

### Key Insights:
-b 4096 -ub 4096: doubles the prompt ingestion from ~150 to 364+ t/s.
-cmoe Free Lunch: Shifting expert layers to DDR4 RAM slashes VRAM from 24GB to 11.6GB with virtually zero decode penalty (22.5 -> 20.9 t/s), enabling the 250k context ceiling.

Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next (UD-Q4_K_XL) is a massive 111.4 GB model split across 4 shards. To run this architecture, you must build from the experimental PR branch (#27742) by @danielhanchen:

git clone && cd llama.cpp 
git fetch origin pull/27742/head:qwen-next && git checkout qwen-next 
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF 
cmake --build build --config Release -j $(nproc) --target llama-server

The open weights TTS crown just moved again.

Breeze TTS 2 officially took the #1 spot among open weight models on the Artificial Analysis TTS leaderboard, surpassing Fish Audio S2 Pro by 90 Elo points and climbing to #6 overall against proprietary frontier systems with a 1,215 Elo.

The problem? Out of the box, the repo targets H100/A100 hardware and enforces Flash Attention 2, instantly crashing if you try running it on free or older consumer GPUs.

So I patched the model config, bypassed the FA2 lock, and built a zero config Google Colab notebook with a live Gradio UI so you can run zero shot voice cloning entirely on a free NVIDIA T4 GPU.

Here is the breakdown of why this model is turning heads and how to run it locally:

# Why Breeze-TTS-2 is a Massive Leap:

- Expressive Vocal Events: Breeze natively executes inline expressive tags. You can literally write (laugh), (sigh), (clears throat), or (cough) directly in your text prompt, and the model performs them naturally.

- Zero Shot Voice Cloning: Captures timbre, cadence, and vocal style from a clean 5–10 second reference audio clip paired with its transcript.

- Voice Direction & Design: Steer tone, pacing, and emotion using natural language prompts (e.g., "Speak slowly with a calm, reflective tone") without losing the identity of the cloned speaker.

- Bilingual Core: Single 3B parameter architecture delivering high fidelity generation across both English and Chinese.

Google Colab’s free T4 GPU uses an older Turing architecture, which physically cannot dispatch Flash Attention 2. Loading the default checkpoint causes an immediate PyTorch environment crash.

By removing the incompatible torchvision dependency and patching the model’s config (flash_attention_2 ➔ eager), we get clean, stable execution:

- Model Size: ~7.68 GB (3B Parameters, Safetensors)
- VRAM Footprint: ~7.7 GiB during eager generation 
- Output: Clean, mono 24 kHz speech synthesis

# Interactive Gradio Web UI
To make this seamless to test, the notebook automatically spins up an interactive Gradio web app directly inside your session:

Discrete math is search over a well defined space, so RL loves it. every step is verifiable, which means a clean reward signal and self play at massive scale.

Physics doesn't offer that oracle. the deeper issue is before you even get to solving anything, physics starts with a mind's eye move. imagining the messy real system and intuiting which idealization captures its essence. Einstein didn't derive Special Relativity by manipulating symbols. he first saw it, riding alongside a light beam, reducing the universe to a train, a platform, a clock. The math came after the vision.

LLMs are blind token manipulators without that inner eye. They can execute the resulting equations flawlessly, but they can't "see" the problem the way a physicist does and even if they could, there's no automatic checker telling them if what they saw was right or interesting. No spatial grounding to generate the idealization, and no verifiable reward to train the instinct even if it existed.

Math gives you a space to search and a way to know you won. Physics asks you to imagine the right space first with no one grading whether you imagined it correctly.

How many API users can you simultaneously host on a single RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM) before it crashes?

Yesterday, I proved you can host 14 active users using unquantized memory. Today, I used 8 bit KV Cache Quantization to hack the VRAM footprint.

I successfully scaled to 24 concurrent users without a single dropped connection. A 71% server capacity boost for free. 

By adding the -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 flags to llama.cpp, you compress the KV cache context memory from 16 bit to 8 bit. This unlocks massive concurrency limits on Gemma 4 26B (MoE) on a single 24GB consumer GPU.

Here is the exact telemetry from pushing 8 bit quantization to its absolute physical edge:

# TEST 1: The 24 User Concurrency Max

Server Config: 24 slots (np 24) | 4,096 context per slot | 98,304 Total Context

Client Load: 24 simultaneous requests (2,000 token prompt per user)

Unquantized KV cache for this load requires 28GB+ VRAM (Instant OOM).

The C++ engine crunched the entire batch in 28.5 seconds.

What happens to a compressed cache during a traffic spike?

Server Config: 24 slots (np 24) | 4,096 context per slot | 98,304 Total Context

Client Load: 48 simultaneous requests (2k token prompt per user)

In my unquantized tests yesterday, single slot prefill was hitting ~1,500+ t/s. Today, under the heavy 48-user Q8 load, prefill dropped as low as ~750 t/s.
